llm.summary: The skill's code and instructions match its stated Planner purpose, but the package/registry metadata omits required credentials and binaries and several instructions are internally inconsistent — review before installing or providing secrets.

dimensions.detail: Name/description and scripts implement Microsoft Graph Planner operations (plans, buckets, tasks) — that capability legitimately needs an Azure AD app and client credentials. However the skill registry metadata lists no required environment variables or primary credential, which contradicts the scripts that expect M365_CLIENT_ID, M365_CLIENT_SECRET, and M365_TENANT_ID in ~/.openclaw/.env.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and the Node scripts instruct the agent to read ~/.openclaw/.env, obtain a client_credentials token from login.microsoftonline.com, and call graph.microsoft.com — all coherent with the stated purpose. There are internal inconsistencies: some docs/scripts mention using the mgc CLI (bash scripts use 'mgc' and 'jq'), while Node scripts do client-credentials directly. The permission names also vary between files (Group.Read.All vs Group.ReadWrite.All, Tasks.ReadWrite.All vs Tasks.ReadWrite).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill is instruction-only in the registry (no install spec), but includes package.json and node scripts and the SKILL.md / CHANGELOG recommend running npm install. Node dependencies are standard Microsoft Graph/axios packages from npm (traceable). No remote arbitrary-download install URLs were used. Risk: the skill will require the user to run npm install (network access) but the registry did not declare this requirement.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The scripts require high‑privilege application credentials (client id/secret/tenant) stored in ~/.openclaw/.env and instruct admin consent for Group and Tasks application permissions — this is proportionate for full Planner CRUD but is sensitive. The registry metadata failing to declare these required env vars and the presence of bash scripts calling external CLIs (mgc, jq) — neither declared as required binaries — are incoherent. Also some instructions request broader permissions (Group.ReadWrite.All) than earlier lines in SKILL.md (Group.Read.All), creating ambiguity about minimal privileges needed.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always: false and no install spec; the skill does not request forced/always-on inclusion nor attempts to modify other skills or system-wide agent settings. It reads a user-local ~/.openclaw/.env file for credentials (normal for CLI tools).
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
This skill appears to do what it says (manage M365 Planner via Graph) but there are important inconsistencies you should address before installing or supplying secrets:

- The code requires sensitive Azure AD application credentials (M365_CLIENT_ID, M365_CLIENT_SECRET, M365_TENANT_ID) stored in ~/.openclaw/.env, but the registry metadata does not declare these environment variables — treat that as a red flag and do not provide secrets until resolved.
- Several bash scripts call external tools (mgc, jq) but the skill declares no required binaries; if you plan to use those scripts, ensure mgc and jq are installed and that their behavior is acceptable.
- The skill requests application-level Graph permissions (admin consent) which grant broad access to Groups and Tasks across the tenant. Only use a least-privilege app in a test tenant first; prefer narrowly scoped permissions and rotate/revoke the client secret after testing.
- The code contacts only Microsoft endpoints (login.microsoftonline.com and graph.microsoft.com) — no hidden external endpoints were found, but confirm by auditing the files yourself.
- Because the source/homepage is unknown, consider cloning the skill into an isolated environment and reviewing/running the scripts in a non-production tenant first. Ask the publisher to update the registry manifest to list required env vars and required binaries, and to correct the permission names so you can assess least-privilege needs.
